  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 4 ## From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360 In Chapter 3, I traced the increasingly widespread association of mucus with Wind disorders from the tenth to the twelfth century and showed that several illnesses whose pathomechanisms had been considered close to those of kuang—Wind strokes and xian 痈 seizures—were often treated with anti-mucus remedies by the end of that period. Let me now explain how the mucus-and-Fire etiology of madness that dominated late-imperial conceptions of insanity developed. The mucus-and-Fire script emerged among doctrinally minded physicians who lived in north China under the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), and was consolidated by southern doctors who were influenced by these northerners in the early fourteenth century under the Yuan dynasty (1260-1368), after the Mongol conquest of both the Jin and the southern Song (1127-1279) had re-established contacts between north and south China. The innovations these medical thinkers proposed built on the trends I outlined in Chapter 3, but it was their doctrinal and therapeutic precepts that came to dominate later medical thinking. During these men's lives (and partly thanks to their efforts), \"Cold Injury\" (shangban 傷寒) replaced \"Wind illnesses\" as the new dominant class of illnesses. The way Jin-Yuan physicians interpreted madness and handled mad people depended on their broader understanding of illness and vitality. The development of Cold- Injury medicine, for example, enhanced the importance of Heat and Fire as etiological factors and motivated a number of doctors to use Cold-Injury remedies to treat psycho- behavioral symptoms. Ni Weide, from Kaifeng, moved to the Suzhou region at some unknown date. He was there in the 1320s looking for a teacher when he found books by Liu Wansu, Zhang Congzheng, and Li Gao. See Wu Yiyi 1993-94: 56-7, citing the Wu county gazetteer (1642; 53.24a-b), Wuzhong renwu zhi 吳中人物志 (1570), and Song Lian's "Gu Ni fujun muzhiming" 故倪府君墓誌銘 (Song Wenxian gong quanji 宋文憲公全集 25.5b-6a). $ ^{148} $ Hua was from Xiangcheng 襄城 (southwest of Kaifeng); he later moved to nearby Yizhen 儀真, and finally to Yuyao 餘姚 (northern Zhejiang, where Xiang Xin's family also lived, at the end of a canal connected to the Grand Canal). The data concerning Hua's moves comes from his biography in History of the Ming (299: 7634-35). Apart from the Basic Questions and the Canon of Problems that his master had made him read, Hua developed his doctrines and skills with the books of Zhang Ji, Liu Wansu, and Li Gao.
